item.title: Ownership Heterogeneity and Knowledge Transfer: Access, Appropriation, and Governance across Organizational Forms
item.content:encoded:
James J. Chrisman, Mississippi State University

Hanqing (Chevy) Fang, Missouri University of Science and Technology

Silvio Vismara, University of Bergamo

Zhenyu Wu, University of Manitoba

This special issue examines how knowledge and technology transfer operate differently across diverse organizational forms, moving beyond the assumption that transfer follows a single institutional model. The call brings together fragmented literature on intellectual property, open innovation, family businesses, and cooperative structures to develop an integrated framework for understanding ownership's role in shaping what knowledge is transferred, retained, or commercialized.

The framework organizes ownership forms along three dimensions: access (who obtains knowledge and on what terms), appropriation (who captures economic returns), and governance (who decides how knowledge is used and protected). These dimensions help explain why knowledge flows differently through universities, private firms, state-owned enterprises, cooperatives, and other organizational structures.

Appel publié par The Journal of Technology Transfer. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Locating and transitioning ownership forms: how family firms, employee-owned firms, SOEs, cooperatives, and platform cooperatives differ in what they transfer and to whom, and how transfer changes as firms professionalize, corporatize, or adopt foundation governance.
  • Hybrid and intermediate arrangements: dual-class structures, stakeholder boards, patent pools, and benefit-corporation statutes, and when such hybrids are stable.
  • University and public research transfer: how technology transfer offices, consortia, and open science initiatives allocate rights, and how policy reforms shift those allocations.
  • AI, data, and platforms: how the three dimensions operate where the asset itself blurs conventional boundaries between use, capture, and control.
  • Rights-based theory, measurement, and policy: work that formalizes the framework, specifies trade-offs, or informs organizational and policy design.

Timeline

  • September 30, 2027: Full paper submission deadline

item.title: Rethinking Technology Transfer: Ensuring Resilience, Economic Impact and Social Value
item.content:encoded:
James A. Cunningham, Newcastle University

Jungho Kim, Newcastle University

Chiara Marzocchi, University of Padua

Natalya Radko, Newcastle University

Technology transfer from universities and industry drives economic development, yet rapidly evolving research and technological advancements require continuous development of effective structures and processes. Universities must balance generating economic impact while supporting social value creation—a challenge operating across macro (government policies), meso (TTO structures), and micro (individual researcher) levels.

Current technology transfer systems face disruptions from technological change, geopolitical shifts, AI emergence, and intellectual property challenges. Universities are increasingly expected to contribute to societal grand challenges alongside traditional commercialisation, creating tensions between economic and social value creation for TTOs and academic entrepreneurs.

This special issue seeks research rethinking technology transfer paradigms to examine how systems can build resilience, become inclusive, and deliver blended value. Papers should address operational challenges, emerging TTO configurations, required capabilities for transfer actors, and how new technologies and policies shape the future of university-industry knowledge transfer.

item.title: Technology Transfer through Collaboration: Bridging Academia, Policy, and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Maksim Belitski, Loyola University New Orleans

James A. Cunningham, Newcastle University

Riccardo Fini, University of Bologna

Simon Mosey, University of Nottingham

Phillip H. Phan, Johns Hopkins University

This special collection seeks research on technology transfer that emerges from collaborative partnerships between academic researchers and non-academic stakeholders such as practitioners, policymakers, and industry professionals. The collection recognizes that such boundary-spanning collaborations provide unique access to emerging phenomena and data that can advance scholarship in the field.

The editors particularly welcome papers co-authored by academics and non-academic actors, including technology transfer professionals, entrepreneurs, investors, and innovation intermediaries. Submissions should demonstrate rigorous methodology while offering meaningful implications for policy and practice, combining novel theoretical contributions with empirical credibility and practical relevance.
